claim: Learned clauses (no-goods) are the single most important CDCL ingredient. Switching learning off cuts solved instances from 9068 to 4837 of 10000 (MiniSat ablation), far more than turning off VSIDS, 2-watched-literals or restarts. Bayardo and Schrag saw plain DP with no look-back fail 100% on hard real-world instances, and Elffers et al. found learned clauses essential for going beyond tree-like proofs.
agent_test: Equal-token A/B on a multi-attempt puzzle set: agent with a persistent short no-good list vs same agent that retries blind; count solved and tokens to solve.

claim: Conflict analysis plus non-chronological backjumping (GRASP 1996) and backjumping plus learning (relsat 1997) were developed separately and let complete solvers finish instances plain DP could not. GRASP solved 149 of 149 BF-1355 instances in 125.7 s total (TEGUS 53 solved). relsat(4) failed 13% of hanoi4 runs vs 100% for naive DP.
agent_test: Compare an agent that, on failure, names which earlier choices caused it and revisits those (backjump) against one that undoes only the last step, at equal tokens.

claim: Practical speed came largely from engineering and decision focus, not new learning theory. Chaff reports more than 90% of time in unit propagation and a one to two order gain from watched literals plus VSIDS. The ablation ranks VSIDS second (6932 solved without it) and watched literals third (8409).
agent_test: Measure the per-step cost of recording and checking no-goods (tokens and time). Keep the check in code.

claim: Unbounded clause storage is costly, so every successful solver bounds retention. GRASP kept clauses of at most 20 literals. relsat relevance-bounded learning beat size-bounded (hanoi4 fail 13% vs 94% and 92%). Glucose LBD-based aggressive deletion solved 176 of 234 vs 132 to 153 for older solvers. Elffers et al. add that over-aggressive erasure hurts when memory is tight.
agent_test: Cap the no-good list by size and relevance (drop entries whose trigger variables have changed). Test list caps of 3, 5, 10 at equal tokens.

claim: Short clauses spanning few decision levels (low LBD, glue clauses) are reused far more than longer ones, and the first-UIP clause has the smallest LBD. This is the main evidence on which no-goods are worth keeping. It is correlational, from SAT-Race and SAT'07 industrial instances.
agent_test: Rank stored lessons by how few separate earlier decisions they involve; keep the shortest first; compare against random retention.

claim: Learning is not a universal win. Look-back gave little on random 3SAT. No DP variant solved the 3bit circuits that WSAT solved trivially. ISAMP was about 10x faster than relsat(4) on six scheduling instances. In MiniSat, families differ: sverif solved 592 without VSIDS vs 420 with full CDCL; termrw solved more with restarts off. Winners are instances with short, easily derived no-goods.
agent_test: Gate the no-good store: use it only where failures repeat (a foothold). Compare tasks with and without repeating dead ends.

claim: Restarts help on average but depend on the family. MiniSat without restarts solved 8653 vs 9068. Luby on gave 4533 SAT and 4535 UNSAT vs 4230 and 4423 off. termrw solved more without restarts (446 vs 420). Clique formulas need restarts off. Heavy-tailed run times justify randomised restarts with a tuned cutoff, but round-robin 14 got worse (411 s vs 17 min).
agent_test: Run several short independent attempts that share one no-good list vs one long attempt, at equal total tokens. Sweep the cutoff.

claim: Restart interval matters and SAT and UNSAT want different settings. Lingeling solved 122 to 168 of 300 as the fixed interval grew from 2 to 256, while UNSAT solved peaked at interval 8 (90). An EMA-based dynamic scheme reached 178 to 181.
agent_test: Adaptive cutoff on attempt length (restart when the recent failure rate rises) vs fixed length.

claim: The decision rule and learning must work together. VSIDS follows variables from recent conflicts and picks bridge variables (adaptVSIDS 351 vs 343 of 1030). A planning-specific heuristic beat VSIDS in the same CDCL solver (757 vs 701 of 968). Branching order supplied from problem structure made pebbling formulas easy for zChaff where learning alone failed.
agent_test: After a failure, bias the next generation toward elements in the newest no-goods (recency weighted) vs uniform. Also test structure-guided ordering.

claim: Proof-complexity theory: clause learning with unlimited restarts is as strong as general resolution, and learning without restarts beats regular and tree-like resolution. These are results for an idealised solver with oracle branching, and the randomised-solver polynomial bound has a huge exponent. They do not predict real speed.
agent_test: Theory only. Use it to justify keeping lessons across restarts, not to predict gains.

claim: An empowerment check on learned clauses (does the clause let unit propagation derive something new) raised UNSAT solved from 402 (Rsat) to 433 (Rsat+) and 438 (Rsat++) on 949 problems, with 34% less time on commonly solved UNSAT. A variant that skipped the check solved 647 vs 740 for plain Rsat.
agent_test: Admit a lesson only if, on replay, it would have changed the failing step (a code check).

claim: The decision level of conflicts falls over a run on most industrial instances (negative slope on 167 of 199 benchmarks; 92% in b10). The fitted finish estimate is about 1.37 times the real conflict count. Correlation only.
agent_test: Track whether failures come earlier across attempts as a progress signal.

claim: Free-text reflections after failure help LLM agents when the failure signal is reliable (ALFWorld 130 of 134; HumanEval 91% vs 80%; Rust 50 hardest 68% vs 60%). They give no gain or harm when the signal is weak (MBPP 0.77 vs 0.80 with 16.3% false-positive tests; Rust without tests 52%). Huang et al. agree: without an oracle, self-correction lowers accuracy (GPT-3.5 CommonsenseQA 75.8 to 41.8 after 5 calls).
agent_test: Write a lesson only when code located a failing output (G2). Compare lesson-on vs lesson-off with a deliberately noisy checker.

claim: Failure lessons kept permanently in context can hurt. Retrieving only the matching lesson at failure time and verifying recovery helped (Sentry WebShop 0.468 vs 0.264 best baseline vs 0.170 unassisted; fixed playbook in persistent context 0.364 to 0.296; removing the intervention-need check cost 54.7% on average). One group, small open model (Qwen3.5-9B), five runs.
agent_test: Store no-goods outside the prompt and inject only entries whose trigger matches the current state. Compare with always-in-context.

claim: Repeating a step that already failed is a common, measured LLM-agent failure. Step repetition is 15.7% of annotated failures (1642 traces, 7 multi-agent systems). Loop ratio is 32.0% for Qwen3-4B in FrozenLake and falls to 1.0% to 5.7% for the 30B model. A no-good filter targets exactly this.
agent_test: Count repeated identical attempts per task with and without a code-level no-good filter.

claim: A solver-style minimal core that says WHICH constraints clash helped in some settings but not others. Core-guided repair beat generic retry on consistency (set consistency 0.91 vs 0.88; revision cost 0.4 vs 0.6; 390 instances) and stopped one model fabricating a solution on infeasible items (1 of 14 vs 11 of 14). Accuracy was equal to generic error feedback (88.3% vs 89.6%, p=1.0). Both samples are small.
agent_test: Return the smallest set of violated constraints from code instead of a bare 'wrong'. Compare repair success at equal tokens.

claim: Localising a failure to the responsible step by counterfactual replacement and keeping a validated minimal edit is feasible (CausalFlow repaired 555 of 1299 failures, 42.7%; range 21.9% to 52.4%). But on MBPP Self-Refine did better (80.3% vs 41.2%) and typed logging cost accuracy on easy tasks (75.0% vs 88.1% direct).
agent_test: Test replace-one-step localisation against reflect-on-whole-trace at equal tokens.

claim: Training on search trees that include failed branches and backtrack instructions made a prover use fewer proof-assistant calls than DFS, and it won at every tried setting out of distribution. In distribution the gap is small (100% vs 99.5% to 99.9%).
agent_test: Needs training, so not usable by a scaffold-only agent. Only the idea of showing failed branches in the prompt carries over.

claim: Prompted LLMs do not carry out SAT-style search reliably. Most say satisfiable for nearly every random 3-SAT formula. Non-reasoning models fall below paired score 0.2 by 25 variables. Small models trained on DPLL traces fail beyond the training size. So the no-good store and its checks should be code, not model reasoning.
agent_test: Keep the no-good list and its subsumption and relevance checks in code. Give the model only the retrieved entries.

claim: LLM-written CDCL heuristics improve solvers on chosen families (AutoSAT beats MiniSat on 9 of 12 datasets and Kissat on 4; ModSAT work reports about 40% PAR-2 gain on its own base). Gains rest on scoring by running code, vanish on some families, and a single tuned solver can still win in-domain.
agent_test: Supports scoring candidates by execution. Not evidence for no-goods.

claim: No paper was found that implements formal no-good learning with backjumping for an LLM agent and measures it against a no-memory baseline. Closest are Reflexion, Sentry, AgentDebug (free-text or playbook lessons) and core-guided repair.
agent_test: Build and test it ourselves. A null result is also informative.

claim: Benefit of stored no-goods depends on how much shorter the derived reason is than the full state. Planning gains ranged 1.6x (blocks world, long memos) to 120x (logistics, short memos), and memo-length reduction tracked speedup; the Bayardo and Schrag boundary is the same.
agent_test: Before enabling a no-good store for a task family, run 5 to 10 failures and have code compute (derived reason size / full state size). Enable only if the ratio is well below 1.

claim: At equal token budgets, free-text reflect-and-repair does not reliably beat simply sampling more fresh attempts; the limit is diagnosis quality. Reflection added 0.05 EM in LATS (HotPotQA) and was generic on WebShop.
agent_test: Any no-good store trial must include a resample-at-equal-tokens arm, not only a no-memory arm.

claim: Backjumping to the true first-mistake step roughly doubles the fix rate over a random cut (word sorting: 23.53% vs 11.76% of wrong traces fixed), but LLMs find that step poorly (GPT-4 52.87 best of five), so the culprit must come from code.
agent_test: Use backjump only where a deterministic check can name the first failing step; otherwise plain retry with a lesson.

claim: A failure or culprit signal must be right about 60 to 70% of the time or more before acting on it beats not acting; below that, correct traces get damaged. Simulated finders: losses plateau near 65%.
agent_test: Measure precision of the failure check on labelled runs. Do not store a no-good from a check below about 70% precision.

claim: Lesson stores can lower scores even for large models when memory is always on, bloated or retrieved too narrowly. DeepSeek-V3.2-Exp AppWorld: 73.2 vanilla vs 64.2 and 44.6 for two memory baselines; GPT-4.1 AppWorld: top-3 retrieval put TGC 2.9 points below baseline. A gated store (accept only if measured net gain) kept the baseline.
agent_test: Gate every store update on a measured gain on a held-out batch and allow an empty store; retrieve by trigger match with a threshold, not by fixed small k.

claim: Restarts pay only when run length is heavy-tailed. Gomes et al. found large gains (logistics.d 108 min deterministic vs about 1,800 backtracks total with restarts) and also one instance with no heavy tail and little gain. No one has measured this for LLM attempt lengths.
agent_test: Log attempt lengths and success per task family; add restarts only if a short fraction of attempts succeeds much faster than the median.

claim: Fresh independent LLM attempts raise coverage roughly log-linearly with sample count (SWE-bench Lite 15.9% to 56% from 1 to 250 samples) when an automatic verifier exists; majority vote or reward models plateau (MATH 40.50% to 41.41%).
agent_test: Spend leftover budget on fresh attempts first when a code verifier exists; the carry-over of lessons has to beat this at equal tokens.

claim: Gains from lesson stores shrink as the base model gets stronger or reasoning is enabled: about +1 point for think-enabled models (AppWorld DeepSeek-Reasoner 75.0 to 76.2). Batch-level abstraction cut memory size 3x while raising accuracy 17% on KaggleDBQA; extra epochs overfit (28.1% to 23.2% test).
agent_test: Keep lessons few, abstract, merged; test whether a lesson store still helps on the final model before shipping it.

claim: Checking stored no-goods can dominate cost. In plain Graphplan memo checking took 11.7 of 19.4 minutes on one instance. Compact no-goods, checked only against the current goal set, avoid this.
agent_test: Keep the store in code and inject only entries whose trigger matches the current state.

claim: A text-only judge is not a safe source of no-goods. No prior work shows self-correction from prompted-LLM feedback except on suited tasks; weak verifiers have high false-positive rates and need aggregation with labels.
agent_test: Feed the store only from code checks (tests, validators). If only judges exist, combine several independent ones and calibrate first.

claim: Still open after the gap search: no paper tests a formal, subsumption-checked no-good store inside an LLM agent against free-text reflection and against resampling at equal tokens (restates K24).
agent_test: Build the three-arm test (no memory, free-text lessons, coded no-goods) on one coded task family where the ratio test of K25 passes.
